vignette:
**Vignette: Rajan, Age 41**

Rajan grew up believing that the police were there to protect people. That belief shattered on a Tuesday afternoon three years ago when he was pulled over while driving home from a client meeting. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated within minutes into something he still cannot fully explain. Two officers ordered him out of the car, pressed him against the hood, and held him there with his arms wrenched behind his back while a third searched his vehicle. No weapon was found. No drugs. Nothing. He was told he matched a description, given a warning for an expired registration sticker he hadn't known about, and released. The officers drove away. Rajan stood on the side of the road for several minutes before he could make himself get back into the car.

He told his wife, Priya, that evening, and she held him while he shook. He told himself it was over. He was wrong.

The weeks that followed brought a kind of internal noise he hadn't known before. He began waking between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, convinced someone was in the house. During the day, certain sounds — a car door slamming, the crackle of a radio — could send a jolt through his chest that left him breathless. He started taking longer routes to avoid the stretch of road where it happened, then longer routes to avoid any road where he'd seen a patrol car recently. His world began to quietly shrink.

Rajan works from a home studio, designing brand identities and marketing materials for small businesses. He has always loved the meditative quality of the work — the way color and composition can communicate something wordless. But in the months after the stop, he found himself staring at his screen for long stretches, unable to concentrate. Deadlines he once met easily began to slip. Clients noticed. He started declining video calls, preferring email, because he didn't trust himself to appear composed. He felt a persistent, low-grade shame about this, as though the incident had exposed something fragile in him that he hadn't known was there.

He has not spoken about it publicly. Among his extended family and his community, there is an unspoken pressure to be grateful, to be successful, to not make trouble. He worries that talking about what happened will make him seem weak, or worse, that people will find some way to suggest he brought it on himself. So he carries it quietly, which means he carries it alone.

Priya knows something is wrong, but Rajan deflects her concern with reassurances he doesn't believe. He has become irritable in ways that confuse him — snapping at her over small things, then feeling flooded with guilt. He avoids television shows featuring police or courtrooms. He has stopped going to the gym he used to love because it requires driving past a police substation. When he does go out, he is acutely aware of any law enforcement presence in a way that exhausts him, his eyes tracking uniformed officers the way an animal tracks a predator.

There are moments, usually late at night, when the memory returns with a physical completeness — the cold metal of the car hood against his cheek, the officer's knee against the back of his leg, the specific quality of his own helplessness. He finds himself wondering what would have happened if he had moved differently, spoken differently, if the situation had gone another way. These thoughts do not resolve. They cycle.

He came to therapy at Priya's gentle insistence, describing the incident in a measured, almost apologetic tone, as though he were afraid of taking up too much space with it. He is articulate and thoughtful. He minimizes. He still drives, still works, still shows up. But there is a wariness behind his eyes now, a vigilance that does not rest, and a man who is quietly grieving the version of himself who once felt safe in the world.
